sections.body: This is a single-outlet pump for nano and small community tanks. It drives one sponge filter, one air stone or a small bubble wall in a tank of up to around 60 litres. For a second device, use a [dual-outlet pump](/product/dual-outlet-air-pump) rather than splitting one outlet, since a split divides an already modest output.

Most air pump noise is vibration, not air. Sit the pump on a soft pad or on its rubber feet, on a flat surface that is not touching the tank stand's hollow panels. Keep it above the waterline and fit a [check valve](/product/bubble-counter-check-valve-set) so that water cannot siphon back if the power fails. If the hum returns after a few months, clean the intake filter and check the diaphragm.

The dial turns the output down for a betta or shrimp tank that does not want a storm. A sponge filter needs only a steady trickle of bubbles to lift water through the foam. If the tank is deep, use the higher setting so that air reaches the stone against the water pressure. If it still struggles, move to a stronger pump.

faqs.q: Can I run it 24 hours a day?
faqs.a: Yes. It is designed for continuous running and draws little power. Clean the intake filter every few months.

faqs.q: Will it drive a bio sponge filter?
faqs.a: Yes. A single sponge filter in a nano tank is the standard pairing for this size of pump.

sections.body: As an Indian almond leaf softens in water it releases tannins, which tint the water amber and soften the light. Bettas, killifish, shrimp and apistogrammas come from blackwater streams where this is normal, and many breed more readily in it. A leaf also grows a film of biofilm as it breaks down, which shrimp and fry graze on, and it gives bettas an anchor under which to build a bubble nest.

Start with one leaf per 40 to 60 litres. Rinse it first, then drop it in, where it floats for a day or two before sinking. Leave it to break down, and replace it when it is eaten through or collapses, usually after a few weeks. For a deeper tea colour, add more leaves or crush one. For clear water, take them out and use [activated carbon](/product/activated-carbon-filter-bags) to remove the tint.

A tank with leaves will look brown and may have a thin film on the surface for the first days. That is biofilm and is harmless. Tannins also soften water slightly and lower pH a little, so check the pH if you keep species that need hard water. In a planted tank the tint reduces the light reaching the plants a little, so watch growth if you use many leaves.

faqs.q: Do I have to boil or soak the leaves first?
faqs.a: A rinse is enough. Soaking in a cup of hot water for a few minutes helps them sink sooner and removes dust, but is not required.

faqs.q: Are they safe for shrimp?
faqs.a: Yes, and shrimp graze on the biofilm that grows on a softening leaf. Use leaves that have no added chemicals.

sections.body: This is a hang-on-back filter for tanks up to about 80 litres, with a flow of 250 litres an hour. That is the right range for a 30 to 80 litre community tank. It hangs on the rim, so it needs no plumbing and no space under the tank, and it is the easy way to add real filtration to a tank that only has room for a rim mount. For a larger tank, look at an internal or a canister.

Water passes through a mechanical sponge that catches debris, a carbon stage that polishes the water, and a biological stage where the bacteria that process ammonia live. After a few weeks you can leave the carbon out and replace it with extra [bio media](/product/ceramic-bio-rings-filter-media), which gives more bacterial surface. Keep the sponge and the biological stage and rinse them gently.

sections.h: Starting it and keeping it quiet
sections.body: Fill the chamber with tank water so the pump primes, and keep the water level above the intake. If the level drops, the motor runs dry and rattles. The flow is adjustable, so turn it down for bettas and slow-water fish. If the waterfall splashes, add a small foam pad under the lip or lower the water level slightly to reduce the sound.

faqs.q: How often should I clean it?
faqs.a: Rinse the sponge in a bucket of tank water every two to four weeks, when flow drops. Never use tap water, and never replace everything at once.

faqs.q: Is it too strong for a betta?
faqs.a: Turn the flow down and, if needed, place a sponge over the outlet or plants near the return. Bettas have long fins and prefer calm water.

sections.h: Built for desks and shrimp cubes
sections.body: This miniature hang-on filter runs from a 5 V USB supply and draws about 2.5 W, so a phone charger or power bank will drive it. It is sized for 10 to 40 litre tanks and hangs on rims that a full hang-on-back would overwhelm. The flow is gentle and arrives through a spray-bar style return, which shrimp and bettas tolerate.

The cartridge tray lifts out for a quick rinse. Swish it in tank water, not tap water, when flow slows. Add a small amount of [ceramic bio media](/product/ceramic-bio-rings-filter-media) to the tray if there is room, so there is more surface for bacteria. Replace the cartridge only when it is worn out and keep part of the old one in place so the bacteria carry across.

A USB power bank gives you a quiet filter that keeps running through a power cut, which is a useful backup for a small tank. Use a decent charger that provides steady 5 V, and keep the plug and the lead dry and off the floor.

faqs.q: Is it strong enough for a 40 litre tank?
faqs.a: It is sized for 10 to 40 litres. At the top of that range, lightly stock the tank and use live plants, or add a second small filter.

faqs.q: Is it safe for baby shrimp?
faqs.a: The flow is gentle, but a sponge over the intake is a good precaution for shrimplets and fry.

sections.body: An inline atomiser sits in the tubing between a canister filter and its outlet, and pushes CO2 through a ceramic disc to make a fine mist. The water carries the mist into the tank, and the CO2 has time to dissolve in the pipe, so little gas escapes at the surface. It suits canister filters with 16 to 22 mm outer-diameter hose. Check your hose before you buy.

Cut the outlet hose and fit the atomiser in line so that the arrow, if marked, points with the flow. Use a hose clamp at each end so that it cannot slip. Connect the CO2 line to the atomiser nipple. A [check valve](/product/bubble-counter-check-valve-set) in the CO2 line stops water from backing up into the regulator when the gas is off.

The disc is replaceable and does not need soaking before use. Over time it clogs with algae and mineral film, which reduces mist and raises the pressure needed. Soak it in a dilute vinegar solution and rinse it well when the mist thins out. It is made of 304 stainless steel, and it also suits air pumps if you want a fine-bubble effect for oxygenation.

faqs.q: Does it work with a regulator?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a diffuser for the CO2 line that runs from a regulator, such as the dual-gauge regulator with solenoid.

faqs.q: Will it fit my filter hose?
faqs.a: It fits tubing of 16 to 22 mm outer diameter. Measure your hose before ordering.

sections.body: This pocket pen reads pH from 0.00 to 14.00 with a resolution of 0.1. It does not measure TDS, hardness or any other parameter. It runs on two 1.5 V cells and calibrates against standard buffer powders. At 0.1 pH it is fine enough to see a CO2 swing or a gradual drift in KH.

Two-point calibration against fresh buffer powder is what keeps a cheap pen honest. Calibrate before important readings and every few weeks otherwise. Rinse the electrode in clean water between solutions and never store it in tap water. Mix fresh buffer each time, because old solution drifts.

Dip the pen into a cup of tank water, let the number settle for a few seconds and note it. Take readings at the same time each day, since pH moves through the day. If you want a faster check of several parameters, use [test strips](/product/test-strips-8-in-1-100-count), and use the pen when you want a closer look at pH alone.

faqs.q: How should I store the pen?
faqs.a: Keep it capped and clean, and never let the electrode dry out or sit in tap water. Follow the care notes that come with the pen.

faqs.q: Why does it read differently from my test strip?
faqs.a: Strips are read by eye against a colour chart and are less precise. Treat the pen as the better pH reading once it has been calibrated.

sections.body: The strip covers pH, general hardness, ammonia nitrogen, nitrate, nitrite, total chlorine, carbonate hardness and total alkalinity. Ammonia and nitrite decide whether a tank is safe for fish. Nitrate tells you when a water change is due. Chlorine is useful for checking tap water. KH and alkalinity are the numbers that move when you inject CO2, and they hold pH steady.

Dip the strip for the time given on the pack, shake off the excess and read it against the chart in good, even light after about 30 seconds. Do not wait too long. Reading too early or late shifts the colour. Test at the same time each week and write down the numbers. A trend tells you more than a single reading.

sections.h: When to use a liquid kit instead
sections.body: Strips are fast and good for a weekly check. If you are chasing a problem, a liquid kit is more precise. For pH alone, a calibrated [pH pen](/product/digital-ph-pen-meter) gives a better number. Keep the tub closed and dry, and use strips within their date, because damp strips give false results.

faqs.q: How long will 100 strips last?
faqs.a: One strip a week for one tank is about two years, though you will use more when cycling a new tank.

faqs.q: How often should I test?
faqs.a: Weekly on an established tank, and every day or two while a new tank is cycling or after a medication course. Write the numbers down so you can see the trend.

sections.body: A sponge filter has no impeller, so nothing is drawn in. Fry, shrimplets and small fish can swim around it safely. Air from a pump rises up the tube, drags water through the foam and pushes it out of the top. The sponge also becomes the biological media once bacteria colonise it, so the filter does both jobs. That is the reason it is the standard for breeding, shrimp and quarantine tanks.

Each filter suits a tank up to about 40 litres, and the pack gives you four. Use one on each small tank, or run two in a larger tank for more surface area. Keep one in an established tank as a spare. If you set up a new tank, move a mature sponge across and the new tank starts with a working colony. You need an [air pump](/product/dual-outlet-air-pump) and airline, which are not included.

Squeeze the sponge in a bucket of old tank water until the brown comes out, then put it back. Tap water kills the bacteria. Clean only one at a time if you run several. A sponge does not need replacing until it falls apart.

faqs.q: Can a sponge filter be the only filter?
faqs.a: In a lightly stocked, planted or breeding tank, yes. For a heavily stocked tank add more sponges or a larger filter.

sections.body: Black plastic intake and outflow pipes are the most visible hardware in a clean aquascape. Glass pipes almost disappear. The outflow curves the water into a rolling movement at the surface, which breaks the surface film and helps gas exchange, and the slotted inflow draws water evenly without pinning small fish against it. The glass is borosilicate, which tolerates temperature changes better than ordinary glass.

The sets come in 12/16 mm and 16/22 mm sizes. Those numbers are the inner and outer diameter of the filter hose. Check the hose that came with your filter, or measure its outer diameter, and order the matching size. If the tubing is wrong, the connectors will leak or slip. The set suits canister and hang-on-back filters and works on rimmed and rimless tanks.

Place the inflow at one end and the outflow at the other to move water across the whole tank. Set the outflow so the curve just breaks the surface, and angle it slightly along the glass. Keep the pipes clear of plants that would grow into them. If you prefer a tougher finish, the [stainless version](/product/steel-lily-pipe-set) takes knocks better.

faqs.q: Is glass more fragile than stainless?
faqs.a: Yes, so handle it carefully when you clean or move equipment. For a tank that gets worked on often, stainless is safer.

faqs.q: Does the surface movement affect CO2?
faqs.a: A strong rolling surface releases CO2 faster. If you run CO2, keep the movement gentle, just enough to keep the surface from going stagnant.

sections.h: When stainless is the better choice
sections.body: Stainless steel pipes have the same shape as glass ones. You give up the invisibility of glass, and in return you can knock them against the rim during a rescape and nothing happens. For a tank that is worked on often, or is somewhere it gets bumped, stainless is the one that survives.

These pipes are 304 stainless steel with a brushed finish, not the cheaper 201 grade, which can spot and stain in fresh water. 304 does not release rust into hardscape. The brushed steel looks deliberate against a rimless tank, but if you want the pipes to vanish, the [glass set](/product/glass-lily-pipe-set) is the better choice.

Choose 12/16 mm or 16/22 mm to match your filter hose. The set includes inflow, outflow and clamps, and suits canister and hang-on-back filters. Position the inflow and outflow at opposite ends so the flow crosses the whole tank. Rinse the pipes before use and clean the inside with a brush from time to time.

Sword plants, crypts, vallisneria and lotus take most of their nutrients through their roots, and a liquid fertiliser barely reaches them. These slow-release capsules sit in the substrate beside the roots and feed them for weeks without adding nitrates to the water column. That is why they do not trigger algae the way heavy liquid dosing can.

Push a capsule into the substrate about 10 to 15 cm apart around each root feeder, deep enough that it does not float up. Do not place them right against fish that dig or in a thin substrate. Refresh them every two to three months, or when the older leaves turn pale. Use them together with a weekly dose of [liquid fertiliser](/product/all-in-one-liquid-fertilizer) for stem plants that feed from the water.

Forty capsules cover several large root feeders for a full cycle or a smaller tank for much longer. In a new tank with fresh [aqua soil](/product/aqua-soil-planted-substrate) you may not need them for the first months, since the soil carries its own supply.

faqs.q: Can I use them with sand or gravel?
faqs.a: Yes, that is where they help most. Inert substrates carry no nutrients, so root feeders depend on tabs or heavy fertilising.

faqs.q: Will they cause algae?
faqs.a: Because the nutrients stay in the substrate, they are less likely to feed algae than water-column dosing. Keep them buried.

sections.body: Dragon stone, also called Ohko stone, is the signature rock of iwagumi layouts. It is warm clay-brown, pitted and textured like scales. The pits hold substrate and moss, so a piece planted with Fissidens or Java moss becomes a living boulder. It is inert, so it does not meaningfully change pH or hardness, which makes it safe for shrimp and soft-water fish.

There are three sizes. 250 g pieces are accents, 500 g is for a small layout, and 1 kg is for feature stones. In a 60 cm tank, a typical layout uses one large stone and two or three smaller ones. Use an odd number of stones with similar grain and angle so the scape looks like a natural rock outcrop, and place the largest stone off centre.

Dust from the quarry washes off in a colander under running water, so rinse before it goes into the tank. Place the stones before you add soil, and bury the lower third so they look anchored. Check the footprint with the [substrate calculator](/tools/substrate-calculator) because rock takes up space that you do not need to fill with soil.

faqs.q: Will it change my water chemistry?
faqs.a: Not in a meaningful way. It is described as an inert clay stone, which is why it suits shrimp and soft-water setups.

faqs.q: How much do I need for a 60 cm tank?
faqs.a: One 1 kg feature stone plus two or three smaller pieces is a typical start. Buy a little extra so you can choose the best arrangement.
